title: A spiral and a star
caption: Spiral galaxy NGC 4900 and a foreground star, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4900 · constellation Virgo · about 45 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, S. J. Smartt, C. Kilpatrick

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A face-on spiral fills the frame, its broken arms built from blue clumps of stars and fine threads of dark dust circling a stubby, pale yellow bar. A broad round disc and a faint halo surround it. On top of the galaxy sits a bright star with long, cross-shaped diffraction spikes.
The two only look close together. The star belongs to our own galaxy and lies just 7109 light-years from Earth, while the spiral, NGC 4900 in Virgo, is about 45 million light-years away.

Hubble built this picture from two of its cameras, the older Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, with observations made more than 20 years apart. Both programs were about how massive stars die. One studied places where supernovae had already gone off, and NGC 4900 made the list because it hosted SN 1999br.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.46 x 2.37 arcminutes) and distance (45 million light years), the frame spans roughly 32,000 × 31,000 light-years. Its light set out about 45 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 contributed images through visible-light B and V filters and a near-infrared I filter (814 nm). The packet does not publish how colors were assigned to the filters.
understand.eye: The 814 nm filter reaches just beyond red light the eye can detect, and a galaxy this far away is far too faint to show such detail to the unaided eye.

explore: The second program photographed more than 150 nearby galaxies ahead of time. When a supernova later appears in one of them, astronomers can look back at these images for the star that exploded, which helps explain how, when and why supernovae happen.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with blue, dust-streaked arms around a pale yellow bar, with a bright foreground star with cross-shaped spikes on top of it.
